architectural_implications.after: Instrument the review/verification stage as the primary capacity metric: review latency, artifact size, human touches per accepted output, queue depth.
architectural_implications.before: Instrument and optimize model throughput: tokens, generations, PRs created, tasks attempted.
architectural_implications.consequence: Schedulers, batching, and agent scope decisions should target reviewer throughput — e.g., capping PR size or task granularity — or the system will generate backlog instead of savings.
architectural_implications.observation: AI acceleration moves the constraint from generation to verification.

architectural_implications.after: Declare a named boundary (allowed inputs, tools, failure paths) and report straight-through success rate inside that boundary separately from assisted/AI-attributed rates.
architectural_implications.before: Report a single blended 'percent automated' figure across all workflow stages.
architectural_implications.consequence: Routing and escalation logic becomes an explicit architectural artifact, and autonomy becomes measurable and comparable across systems.
architectural_implications.observation: Autonomy claims need a declared operating boundary.

architectural_implications.after: Maintain a calibration set of expert ground-truth decisions with inter-expert agreement, and track escaped defects alongside judge scores.
architectural_implications.before: Use an LLM-as-judge or rubric score as the reliability metric for the agent.
architectural_implications.consequence: Eval harness must include a human-anchored calibration layer and an escape-analysis loop; judge scores reported with a measured optimism offset.
architectural_implications.observation: Automated graders are biased optimistic proxies for expert acceptance.

architectural_implications.after: Compute cost per accepted autonomous task, loading AI inference + human review + rework + escalation into the numerator.
architectural_implications.before: Compute cost per generated task or per AI-touched task.
architectural_implications.consequence: Changes which workflows are worth automating: high straight-through-rate, low-rework tasks get prioritized; attractive-looking high-volume tasks with expensive review may be net negative.
architectural_implications.observation: Rework and escalation are hidden costs of automation.

article_ideas.angle: Take the highest-profile public automation percentage available and show that it is fully consistent with near-zero autonomy, then show what the boundary-based restatement would have to contain.
article_ideas.audience: Engineers and technical leaders building or procuring agentic systems, plus investors reading AI decks
article_ideas.based_on: AI-attributed and autonomous are distinct claims.
article_ideas.thesis: A single automation percentage is an unfalsifiable metric because it conflates AI-attributed assistance with straight-through autonomous execution; the only defensible claim is a success rate inside a declared operating boundary, reported separately from attribution rate.
article_ideas.title: Your 70% Automated Is a Ladder, Not a Number

article_ideas.angle: Use the +98% PRs / +91% review time / +154% PR size telemetry to argue that every generate-then-verify pipeline (code, docs, tickets, data fixes) has the same shape, and derive concrete design consequences: artifact size caps, task granularity, and reviewer-throughput metrics.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and DevEx engineers, engineering managers, AI product architects
article_ideas.based_on: making code production cheaper increases the volume and size of work entering human review
article_ideas.thesis: Accelerating artifact generation does not reduce required labor; it converts labor into a larger, slower verification queue, so capacity planning must size the reviewer stage first and treat generation throughput as an input to that queue rather than the headline result.
article_ideas.title: The Bottleneck Is the Verifier: Why Cheaper Generation Makes Review the Binding Constraint

article_ideas.angle: Frame the 24.2-point grader-versus-maintainer gap as a measurable bias term rather than an anecdote, then specify the calibration layer: expert-labeled ground truth, inter-expert agreement, and escape tracking.
article_ideas.audience: ML/eval engineers, AI reliability leads, technical due diligence practitioners
article_ideas.based_on: Automated graders are often substantially more optimistic than human maintainers.

connections.relationship: Autonomy is only measurable relative to a declared boundary and success criterion, making the boundary an architectural artifact rather than a marketing qualifier.
Eval credibility is anchored on independent expert acceptance decisions and escape analysis, not on judge scores.
Unit economics restructured around accepted output, with review and rework loaded as cost terms.
Cheap generation increases work-in-progress entering verification, so system throughput is governed by verifier capacity.
A high attribution percentage is consistent with near-zero autonomy; the metrics are not substitutes.

evidence_quotes.text: Observational telemetry of 10,000+ developers showed 98% more merged PRs but 91% longer PR review time and 154% larger PR size.
More work entering the system often increases the downstream review queue burden.
High AI adoption increases PR volume, review time, and PR size, which expands review labor requirements rather than reducing headcount.

core_insights.generalization: In any generate-then-verify pipeline (code, documents, tickets, data fixes), optimizing the generator relocates the bottleneck to the verifier; system throughput is governed by verification capacity and artifact size.
core_insights.insight: Cheap AI generation shifts the bottleneck downstream: making code production cheaper increases the volume and size of work entering human review, so the constraint moves to reviewer labor rather than disappearing. The telemetry cited shows output volume rising far faster than review capacity, meaning net labor savings must be measured at the review stage, not the generation stage.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Any system that generates artifacts faster than humans can verify them will saturate on verification. Architecture and capacity planning should size the review/verification stage first and treat generation throughput as an input to that queue, not the headline metric.

evidence_quotes.text: Automation claims sit on a spectrum from AI drafted with human in the loop to straight-through processing inside a named boundary.
AI-attributed and autonomous are distinct claims.
Uber's claim that >70% of pull requests are AI-attributed.

core_insights.generalization: Autonomy should be expressed as a success rate inside a declared operating boundary (inputs, tools, failure handling), not as a percentage of work touched by AI.
core_insights.insight: 'Automation' is not binary but a ladder: AI-drafted-with-human-in-the-loop at one end and straight-through processing inside a named boundary at the other. 'AI-attributed' output and 'autonomous' execution are categorically different claims, so a single percentage conflates rungs of the ladder.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Agentic system design needs an explicit, named boundary that defines where human intervention is required and where execution is truly straight-through. Without that boundary, autonomy claims are unfalsifiable and the system's operating envelope is undefined.

evidence_quotes.text: Automated graders are often substantially more optimistic than human maintainers.
METR study showing a 24.2 percentage-point gap between automated grader scores and maintainer merge decisions.
Always verify who labeled ground truth, whether experts agree, and what bad output escaped.

core_insights.generalization: Model-as-judge evaluation must be calibrated against independent expert ground truth; the judge's optimism is a measurable bias term, not noise.
core_insights.insight: Automated graders systematically overstate success relative to human expert acceptance decisions; the reported gap between grader scores and maintainer merge decisions was 24.2 percentage points. This implies benchmark/eval score is a biased proxy for the outcome the business actually consumes.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If your eval harness is the same model family or rubric that generated the output, its ceiling is inflated. Calibration against an independent expert acceptance decision, plus tracking of what bad output escaped, is required before trusting any eval-derived reliability number.

evidence_quotes.text: A warning or due diligence flag is not enough unless it translates into financial unit economics.
Failed, escalated, or reworked tasks belong in the cost bucket.
Minus AI + review + rework cost

core_insights.generalization: Any automation ROI model should use cost-per-accepted-output as the unit, with rework and escalation as first-class cost terms rather than excluded externalities.
core_insights.insight: The correct denominator for AI unit economics is the accepted autonomous task, not the attempted or generated one. The P&L bridge multiplies eligible workflow value by adoption rate, straight-through success, and accepted quality, then subtracts AI cost plus review cost plus rework cost — placing failures, escalations, and rework explicitly in the cost bucket.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It converts a technical metric into a per-unit cost figure that can be compared against fully loaded human labor, and it prevents the common error of amortizing AI inference cost across generated tasks while ignoring the human review and rework that generation induces.

evidence_quotes.text: A controlled experiment showing 55.8% faster development on a single JavaScript HTTP server.
Control experiment with 95 professional developers building a JavaScript HTTP server against 12 visible tests.
Controlled lab tasks do not reflect messy, long-horizon production environments.

core_insights.generalization: Benchmark gains measured on short-horizon tasks with fully visible acceptance criteria systematically overstate gains on long-horizon tasks with hidden requirements.
core_insights.insight: Headline productivity numbers often originate in tightly scoped lab conditions — a single JavaScript HTTP server built by 95 professional developers against 12 visible tests — and do not transfer to long-horizon, messy production work. The scope of the original experiment is the hidden variable behind the headline figure.
core_insights.why_it_matters: When evaluating any agent benchmark or vendor claim, the scope of the task (visible tests, single artifact, short horizon) is the strongest predictor of whether the gain will reproduce in production. Reporting should include task scope and visibility of the acceptance criteria.

evidence_quotes.text: Evaluation maturity is the first credibility signal to look for.
Ask for 18 months of workload volume compared against fully loaded human labor.

core_insights.generalization: Credibility of an AI system is gated on eval quality; instrumenting human touches over a long window is a precondition for any credible automation claim.
core_insights.insight: Evaluation maturity should be checked first, ahead of architecture or financial claims, because it determines whether any other number in the deck can be trusted. Diligence sequence: arithmetic (volume vs labor over ~18 months, counting every human touch), definition (which rung of autonomy), then the tell (who defines quality).
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives an explicit ordering for technical vetting of an AI system, and inverts into a build principle: invest in eval maturity and human-touch instrumentation before claiming or scaling autonomy.

More work entering the system often increases the downstream review queue burden.

project_ideas.poc: A synthetic generate-then-verify pipeline where an LLM produces code/doc artifacts at configurable volume and size, a simulated reviewer with finite per-hour capacity and size-dependent review latency accepts or rejects them, and generation volume and max artifact size are swept across a grid.

project_ideas.based_on: the judge's optimism is a measurable bias term, not noise

project_ideas.name: Judge-Optimism Meter

project_ideas.based_on: straight-through processing inside a named boundary

project_ideas.poc: A spec-and-instrumentation harness: a declarative boundary file (allowed inputs, tools, failure paths, acceptance criteria) plus a runtime ledger that tags every task as straight-through, escalated, reworked, or rejected, emitting a per-boundary success rate alongside the legacy blended percentage.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Soukaïna Abelhad
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Evaluating AI automation claims and productivity metrics during technical due diligence
  • Purpose: Provide investors and technical leaders with a robust framework (the diligence card) to critically evaluate AI startup productivity claims, automation rates, and P&L impact. Soukaïna Abelhad shares insights from conducting technical due diligence on AI startups, explaining how to evaluate metrics like '55.8% faster' and '70% automated' through three critical checks: arithmetic, definition, and the tell. She explains how high AI adoption often increases human review workload and why financial translation of metrics is essential for investors and operators.

Topic Map

Introduction to AI Technical Due Diligence

  • Explanation: Introduction of the speaker and the premise of technical due diligence when encountering inflated AI automation metrics.
  • Key claims:
    • AI decks frequently cite impressive productivity and automation numbers.
    • Due diligence requires verifying whether the numbers support the conclusions drawn.
  • Examples:
    • A controlled experiment showing 55.8% faster development on a single JavaScript HTTP server.
  • Terminology:
    • technical due diligence
    • controlled experiment
    • AI adoption
  • Why it matters: Helps distinguish between genuine productivity gains and marketing hype.

Check 1: The Arithmetic

  • Explanation: Examining whether increased AI output translates to reduced head count or simply increased downstream review workload.
  • Key claims:
    • More work entering the system often increases the downstream review queue burden.
    • Observational telemetry of 10,000+ developers showed 98% more merged PRs but 91% longer PR review time and 154% larger PR size.
  • Examples:
    • Faros AI study showing increased PR volume leading to a bottleneck in human review labor.
  • Terminology:
    • observational telemetry
    • PR review time
    • human labor tracking
  • Why it matters: Proves that AI acceleration often shifts work rather than eliminating it.

Check 2: The Definition

  • Explanation: Dissecting what 'automation' actually means by examining the spectrum from AI drafted to zero human intervention.
  • Key claims:
    • Automation claims sit on a spectrum from AI drafted with human in the loop to straight-through processing inside a named boundary.
    • AI-attributed and autonomous are distinct claims.
  • Examples:
    • Uber's claim that >70% of pull requests are AI-attributed.
  • Terminology:
    • straight-through processing
    • AI-attributed
    • human-in-the-loop
  • Why it matters: Prevents confusing assisted work with autonomous execution.

Check 3: The Tell

  • Explanation: Comparing automated evaluation results against human expert merge decisions to check evaluation maturity.
  • Key claims:
    • Automated graders are often substantially more optimistic than human maintainers.
    • Evaluation maturity is the first credibility signal to look for.
  • Examples:
    • METR study showing a 24.2 percentage-point gap between automated grader scores and maintainer merge decisions.
  • Terminology:
    • automated grader
    • maintainer merge decision
    • ground truth
  • Why it matters: Uncovers discrepancies between model benchmarks and expert judgment.

The P&L Bridge and Financial Translation

  • Explanation: Translating technical metrics into unit economics by calculating the cost per accepted autonomous task.
  • Key claims:
    • A warning or due diligence flag is not enough unless it translates into financial unit economics.
    • Failed, escalated, or reworked tasks belong in the cost bucket.
  • Examples:
    • Engineer.ai (Builder.ai) public warning by WSJ in 2019, revenue estimate cuts in 2025, and Chapter 7 filing.
  • Terminology:
    • P&L bridge
    • cost per accepted autonomous task
    • straight-through success
  • Why it matters: Ensures AI investments survive both technical validation and financial scrutiny.

Key Points

Volume vs. Labor Arithmetic

  • Explanation: High AI adoption increases PR volume, review time, and PR size, which expands review labor requirements rather than reducing headcount.
  • Evidence: Telemetry from 10,000+ developers showing +98% merged PRs, +91% review time, and +154% PR size.
  • Practical implication: Ask for 18 months of workload volume compared against fully loaded human labor.

Defining Automation Boundaries

  • Explanation: Companies conflate AI assistance with autonomous execution. True straight-through processing requires a defined boundary with zero human intervention.
  • Evidence: Uber's >70% AI-attributed PR metric vs. distinct workflow stages (drafted, edited, approved, no human intervention).
  • Practical implication: Clarify where on the spectrum the automation claim sits.

Evaluation Maturity Gap

  • Explanation: Automated evaluation benchmarks often vastly overstate success compared to human domain experts.
  • Evidence: METR findings showing a 24.2 percentage-point gap between automated graders and human maintainers.
  • Practical implication: Always verify who labeled ground truth, whether experts agree, and what bad output escaped.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Dilgence Card (Three Checks)

  • How it works: Three rigorous checks applied to AI productivity and automation claims before accepting them in financial or technical evaluations.
  • Components:
    • Arithmetic: Volume vs. labor (18 months, count every human touch)
    • Definition: Which rung? (Assisted, approved, or straight-through)
    • The Tell: Who defines quality? (Ground truth, agreement, judge, escapes)
  • When to use: During technical due diligence, vendor evaluations, or investment reviews of AI companies.

The P&L Bridge

  • How it works: Formula to translate workflow value into captured economic value by factoring in adoption, success, quality, and rework costs.
  • Components:
    • Eligible workflow value
    • Adoption rate
    • Straight-through success
    • Accepted quality
    • Minus AI + review + rework cost
  • When to use: When projecting financial returns or unit economics on AI-driven operational efficiency.

Examples & Case Studies

Control experiment with 95 professional developers building a JavaScript HTTP server against 12 visible tests.

  • Illustrates: The origin of the '55.8% faster' claim often cited in marketing decks.
  • Lesson: Controlled lab tasks do not reflect messy, long-horizon production environments.

METR study comparing automated graders against maintainer merge decisions across 296 AI pull requests.

  • Illustrates: The 24.2 percentage-point gap between automated benchmark scores and human expert acceptance.
  • Lesson: Automated evaluation maturity must be tested against expert human review.

Builder.ai (Engineer.ai) faced WSJ questioning in 2019, revenue estimate cuts from $220M to $55M in May 2025, and filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2025.

  • Illustrates: How failing to turn public warnings into strict diligence gates leads to insolvency driven by financial and operational realities beyond AI claims.
  • Lesson: A warning is not a diligence gate; even if a claim survives technical checks, it must survive unit economics.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Count every human touch in the workflow rather than just looking at raw code generation volume.
    • Determine whether automation claims refer to AI assistance or zero-intervention straight-through processing.
  • Strategic:
    • Use the P&L bridge framework to calculate cost per accepted autonomous task.
    • Evaluate AI maturity by checking automated test results against expert human review data.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • Who labeled the ground truth for evaluation datasets?
    • What percentage of AI-generated output escapes into production without human review?
    • How do downstream review bottlenecks scale with increased AI-generated workload?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • High AI adoption teams merge 98% more pull requests with a 91% increase in review time. (statistical observation)
  • Automated graders score higher than human maintainer merge decisions by a 24.2 percentage-point gap. (empirical research finding)

Notable Quotes

"A true number can answer the wrong question" "The warning existed. The process did not turn it into a gate." "The job of diligence is not to ask whether the number is impressive. It's to ask what must be true for the number to matter."

Compressed Summary

  • Technical due diligence must test arithmetic, definitions, and evaluation maturity of AI claims.
  • Increased AI code generation volume frequently creates downstream human review bottlenecks.
  • Financial translation via P&L bridges connects workflow adoption to unit economics like cost per accepted autonomous task.
  • Keywords: due diligence, ai automation, productivity metrics, unit economics, evaluation maturity
  • Core insight: Evaluating AI productivity claims requires looking past raw generation volume to measure downstream review labor, strict automation definitions, and true unit economic impact.

  - technical due diligence
  - controlled experiment
  - AI adoption
- **Why it matters**: Helps distinguish between genuine productivity gains and marketing hype.
### Check 1: The Arithmetic
- **Explanation**: Examining whether increased AI output translates to reduced head count or simply increased downstream review workload.
- **Key claims**:
  - More work entering the system often increases the downstream review queue burden.
  - Observational telemetry of 10,000+ developers showed 98% more merged PRs but 91% longer PR review time and 154% larger PR size.
- **Examples**:
  - Faros AI study showing increased PR volume leading to a bottleneck in human review labor.
- **Terminology**:
  - observational telemetry
  - PR review time
  - human labor tracking
- **Why it matters**: Proves that AI acceleration often shifts work rather than eliminating it.
### Check 2: The Definition
- **Explanation**: Dissecting what 'automation' actually means by examining the spectrum from AI drafted to zero human intervention.
- **Key claims**:
  - Automation claims sit on a spectrum from AI drafted with human in the loop to straight-through processing inside a named boundary.
  - AI-attributed and autonomous are distinct claims.
- **Examples**:
  - Uber's claim that >70% of pull requests are AI-attributed.
- **Terminology**:
  - straight-through processing
  - AI-attributed
  - human-in-the-loop
- **Why it matters**: Prevents confusing assisted work with autonomous execution.
### Check 3: The Tell
- **Explanation**: Comparing automated evaluation results against human expert merge decisions to check evaluation maturity.
- **Key claims**:
  - Automated graders are often substantially more optimistic than human maintainers.
  - Evaluation maturity is the first credibility signal to look for.
- **Examples**:
  - METR study showing a 24.2 percentage-point gap between automated grader scores and maintainer merge decisions.
- **Terminology**:
  - automated grader
  - maintainer merge decision
  - ground truth
- **Why it matters**: Uncovers discrepancies between model benchmarks and expert judgment.
### The P&L Bridge and Financial Translation
- **Explanation**: Translating technical metrics into unit economics by calculating the cost per accepted autonomous task.
- **Key claims**:
  - A warning or due diligence flag is not enough unless it translates into financial unit economics.
  - Failed, escalated, or reworked tasks belong in the cost bucket.
- **Examples**:
  - Engineer.ai (Builder.ai) public warning by WSJ in 2019, revenue estimate cuts in 2025, and Chapter 7 filing.
- **Terminology**:
  - P&L bridge
  - cost per accepted autonomous task
  - straight-through success
- **Why it matters**: Ensures AI investments survive both technical validation and financial scrutiny.
## Key Points
### Volume vs. Labor Arithmetic
- **Explanation**: High AI adoption increases PR volume, review time, and PR size, which expands review labor requirements rather than reducing headcount.
- **Evidence**: Telemetry from 10,000+ developers showing +98% merged PRs, +91% review time, and +154% PR size.
- **Practical implication**: Ask for 18 months of workload volume compared against fully loaded human labor.
### Defining Automation Boundaries
- **Explanation**: Companies conflate AI assistance with autonomous execution. True straight-through processing requires a defined boundary with zero human intervention.
- **Evidence**: Uber's >70% AI-attributed PR metric vs. distinct workflow stages (drafted, edited, approved, no human intervention).
- **Practical implication**: Clarify where on the spectrum the automation claim sits.
### Evaluation Maturity Gap
- **Explanation**: Automated evaluation benchmarks often vastly overstate success compared to human domain experts.
- **Evidence**: METR findings showing a 24.2 percentage-point gap between automated graders and human maintainers.
- **Practical implication**: Always verify who labeled ground truth, whether experts agree, and what bad output escaped.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Dilgence Card (Three Checks)
- **How it works**: Three rigorous checks applied to AI productivity and automation claims before accepting them in financial or technical evaluations.
- **Components**:
  - Arithmetic: Volume vs. labor (18 months, count every human touch)
  - Definition: Which rung? (Assisted, approved, or straight-through)
  - The Tell: Who defines quality? (Ground truth, agreement, judge, escapes)
- **When to use**: During technical due diligence, vendor evaluations, or investment reviews of AI companies.
### The P&L Bridge
- **How it works**: Formula to translate workflow value into captured economic value by factoring in adoption, success, quality, and rework costs.
- **Components**:
  - Eligible workflow value
  - Adoption rate
  - Straight-through success
  - Accepted quality
  - Minus AI + review + rework cost
- **When to use**: When projecting financial returns or unit economics on AI-driven operational efficiency.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Control experiment with 95 professional developers building a JavaScript HTTP server against 12 visible tests.
- **Illustrates**: The origin of the '55.8% faster' claim often cited in marketing decks.
- **Lesson**: Controlled lab tasks do not reflect messy, long-horizon production environments.
### METR study comparing automated graders against maintainer merge decisions across 296 AI pull requests.
- **Illustrates**: The 24.2 percentage-point gap between automated benchmark scores and human expert acceptance.
- **Lesson**: Automated evaluation maturity must be tested against expert human review.
### Builder.ai (Engineer.ai) faced WSJ questioning in 2019, revenue estimate cuts from $220M to $55M in May 2025, and filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in June 2025.
- **Illustrates**: How failing to turn public warnings into strict diligence gates leads to insolvency driven by financial and operational realities beyond AI claims.
- **Lesson**: A warning is not a diligence gate; even if a claim survives technical checks, it must survive unit economics.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Count every human touch in the workflow rather than just looking at raw code generation volume.
  - Determine whether automation claims refer to AI assistance or zero-intervention straight-through processing.
- **Strategic**:
  - Use the P&L bridge framework to calculate cost per accepted autonomous task.
  - Evaluate AI maturity by checking automated test results against expert human review data.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - Who labeled the ground truth for evaluation datasets?
  - What percentage of AI-generated output escapes into production without human review?
  - How do downstream review bottlenecks scale with increased AI-generated workload?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- High AI adoption teams merge 98% more pull requests with a 91% increase in review time. (statistical observation)
- Automated graders score higher than human maintainer merge decisions by a 24.2 percentage-point gap. (empirical research finding)
## Notable Quotes
> "A true number can answer the wrong question"
> "The warning existed. The process did not turn it into a gate."
> "The job of diligence is not to ask whether the number is impressive. It's to ask what must be true for the number to matter."
## Compressed Summary
- Technical due diligence must test arithmetic, definitions, and evaluation maturity of AI claims.
- Increased AI code generation volume frequently creates downstream human review bottlenecks.
- Financial translation via P&L bridges connects workflow adoption to unit economics like cost per accepted autonomous task.
- **Keywords**: due diligence, ai automation, productivity metrics, unit economics, evaluation maturity
- **Core insight**: Evaluating AI productivity claims requires looking past raw generation volume to measure downstream review labor, strict automation definitions, and true unit economic impact.
